name: Noname
label: Self-released
lede: Fatimah Warner grew up around her mother's Bronzeville bookstore, finished her first mixtape in two rented Airbnbs, built a book club that ships to prisons, and put out her second album herself in 2023.

eras.title: A bookstore kid from Bronzeville
eras.text: Fatimah Warner grew up on Chicago's South Side and spent her time in her mother's Afrocentric bookstore. Poetry came before rap, and the Chicago scene she came up in (YOUMedia, slam, open mics) is where her circle formed.

years.h: Fatimah Warner is born in Bronzeville
years.p: Her grandparents, both entrepreneurs, raise her until middle school. Then she moves in with her mother, who runs an Afrocentric bookstore.
years.xp: Wikipedia says she listened to the blues players Buddy Guy and Howlin' Wolf as a teenager and spent hours in her mother's shop. The bookstore later closed. She has pointed to that loss when explaining why her own book club backs independent sellers.

years.h: A third-place slam finish, then rapping as Noname Gypsy
years.p: A high school creative writing class turns her toward poetry. She places third at Louder Than a Bomb, Chicago's teen slam festival, and starts rapping as Noname Gypsy.
years.xp: She spent time at YOUMedia, the teen digital-arts space inside the Harold Washington Library. That is where she befriended [[Chance the Rapper|373a4c98-a46b-48e4-86ec-f6ca65b4f438]] and met the experimental rapper LUCKI, per Wikipedia.

eras.title: The verse everyone rewound
eras.text: Before she had a project of her own, Noname kept turning up inside other people's records. Chicago's mixtape class of the early 2010s kept calling her.

years.h: Her verse on 'Lost' puts her on Chance the Rapper's Acid Rap
years.p: It is her first wide exposure. She turns up on Mick Jenkins's The Waters in 2014 and Kirk Knight's Late Knight Special in 2015.

eras.title: Telefone, and a name with nothing attached
eras.text: The mixtape she had been announcing since 2012 finally lands, free, and Chicago's new soul-rap wave has a face. She also drops 'Gypsy' for good.

years.h: Noname Gypsy drops the Gypsy
years.p: She learns the word is a slur for Romani people and cuts it. The new name, she says, is about not being boxed in.
years.xp: Wikipedia quotes her explaining the change: 'Noname could potentially be a nurse. Noname could be a screenwriter.' The mixtape she was working on had been announced under the old name in 2012.

years.h: Telefone goes up free on Bandcamp, four years after it was announced
years.p: Ten tracks built around phone calls, with [[Saba|057d211a-fba8-42d7-ad14-41f41d6f762f]], [[Smino|96800e05-9924-4321-859a-76e0d4750f2f]] and [[Eryn Allen Kane|8c94a5be-2932-477f-80f8-0a07c850cd78]] on guest spots. Pitchfork called it a 'stunning debut' and gave it 8.0.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says Noname told an interviewer in January 2014 that finishing depended on whether she could afford mixing. In June 2016 she moved to Los Angeles with her production team and set up makeshift studios in two Airbnb rentals to finish it. [[Phoelix|c9a8ee10-c27e-4b78-90a9-0b5a230e7941]] and Cam O'bi were the executive producers, with [[Saba|057d211a-fba8-42d7-ad14-41f41d6f762f]] and Monte Booker also producing.

Pitchfork ranked it No. 27 among its 50 best albums of 2016, and Stereogum put it at No. 28. The cover was hand-painted by Nikko Washington of the Chicago collective SaveMoney. Vinyl pressings came in September 2017.

years.h: Five months after Telefone, she's on Saturday Night Live
years.p: Noname appears with [[Chance the Rapper|373a4c98-a46b-48e4-86ec-f6ca65b4f438]] on SNL in December 2016.

years.h: She brings a four-piece band to NPR's Tiny Desk
years.p: Five Telefone songs: 'Diddy Bop', 'Yesterday', 'Reality Check', 'Casket Pretty' and 'Bye Bye Baby'.

eras.title: Room 25 and a second job
eras.text: She makes the album people had waited for, then starts a book club that becomes the more consuming project. A second album is announced and does not arrive.

years.cap: Noname at Electric Forest, Michigan, July 2018
years.h: Room 25 comes out of one summer and a pile of tour money
years.p: Named for the hotel rooms she lived in at 25 in Los Angeles. Pitchfork gave it 8.6 and Best New Music.
years.xp:
Wikipedia dates the recording to July through September 2018, with [[Phoelix|c9a8ee10-c27e-4b78-90a9-0b5a230e7941]] as principal producer and Luke Titus and Brian Sanborn on select tracks. It was self-funded from touring proceeds. Noname told The Fader: 'I needed to make an album because I need to pay my rent.'

Pitchfork's Briana Younger called it 'a transcendent coming-of-age tale built around cosmic jazz and neo-soul.' Pitchfork ranked it No. 15 of 2018, and Robert Christgau later called it the fifth-best album of the 2010s.

years.h: Room 25 goes to network TV on The Late Show with Stephen Colbert
years.p: She brings the album to Colbert about a month after it comes out.

years.h: Factory Baby is announced as album number two
years.p: She will cancel it in December 2021, saying she struggled to find producers she connected with sonically.

years.cap: Noname at the Showbox, Seattle, March 9, 2019
years.h: A fan reading Jackson Rising gives Noname a book club
years.p: The first picks are Paulo Freire's Pedagogy of the Oppressed and Samantha Irby's We Are Never Meeting in Real Life.
years.xp:
Wikipedia says the club began when a fan noted they were reading the same book she was. It picks two books a month and steers readers toward local, POC-owned bookstores. Noname described it as 'a little bit of a fuck you to Amazon', per Wikipedia.

By 2023, Wikipedia counts donations to more than 400 prison facilities. The Mary Sue reports the Prison Program ships over 600 books a month.

years.h: Noname, Saba and Smino release one song as Ghetto Sage
years.p: 'Häagen Dazs' arrives in October 2019. The three reunite on Noname's Tiny Desk in 2023.

years.big: 'I refuse to keep making music and putting it online for free for people who won't support me.'
years.h: Noname says she might quit over who is buying her music
years.p: She voices frustration with her largely white audience and considers walking away, according to Wikipedia.

eras.title: Less music, more work
eras.text: A stretch defined by what she did not release. Politics, organizing and the book club take over her calendar, and an album is announced, delayed and cancelled.

years.h: Noname invents Library Card Registration Day
years.p: She sets January 11 as a day to sign up for a library card, and criticizes Amazon's 'consumer model' while doing it.

years.big: 'My ego got the best of me.'
years.h: Noname answers J. Cole's 'Snow on tha Bluff' with 'Song 33'
years.p: Madlib produces the reply, which is about violence against Black women. It lands two days after Cole's song seemed to take a shot at her activism.
years.xp:
Wikipedia notes the track reflected on Oluwatoyin Salau's death. Noname later wrote that she was not proud of responding with it, apologized for the distraction, and said she was leaving it up, per NME. She donated her proceeds to Black mutual aid funds.

NME reports Cole never confirmed the song was about her. He later said he honors her as a leader in the reading and learning.

years.h: She turns down the Judas and the Black Messiah soundtrack
years.p: After seeing the film, Noname declines the offer and criticizes it for not centering Fred Hampton's 'radical communist politics'.

years.h: The Radical Hood Library opens in Los Angeles
years.p: The Book Club's free library and prison-book shipping hub gives Black and Brown neighbors first call on RSVPs.

years.h: Factory Baby is cancelled and the music goes on hold
years.p: Noname says on Instagram that the album is off and she is taking an indefinite break.
years.xp: She had said earlier that political education and organizing were pulling her away. The Nation quotes her: 'a little less interested in making music.' Her book club had grown into chapters across the US and a prison program.

years.h: A festival booking and home-studio photos hint she's working again
years.p: Pitchfork Music Festival lists her for July, and the next day she posts home-studio photos. In April she is added to Afropunk and says an album would follow a few shows.

eras.title: Sundial, on her own terms
eras.text: A festival lineup, a controversy over one guest verse, an album, and a block party in the neighborhood that raised her. Pitchfork ranks the record No. 13 of the year.

years.h: Coachella 2023 puts her name on a lineup again
years.p: It is the first big festival lineup with her name on it since the 2021 cancellation.

years.h: Factory Baby turns into Sundial
years.p: Noname announces the record with a July target and says she is releasing it herself.

years.src: Wikipedia: Sundial (album) · Wikipedia: Noname (rapper) · The Hurst Review
years.h: The 'Balloons' single is pulled after a day
years.p: Noname announces 'Balloons' with [[Jay Electronica|8bf283b9-b1e2-4632-a953-eacd212a543e]] and [[Eryn Allen Kane|8c94a5be-2932-477f-80f8-0a07c850cd78]] for July 21. Backlash over Electronica erupts, and the single release is cancelled.
years.xp:
Wikipedia reports the backlash centered on Jay Electronica's antisemitism accusations and his comments about the Ukraine war on the track. She defended the collaboration on Twitter before deleting her account two days later. She contemplated shelving the whole album, per the Sundial article. The track was on the final record anyway.

The Hurst Review's Aug. 17 roundup notes Noname 'has refused calls to apologize'.

q: a cool and masterful interrogation of the culture
years.src: Album of the Year · BrooklynVegan · The Nation · Wikipedia: Sundial (album)
years.h: She releases Sundial herself, 31 minutes and 50 seconds of it
years.p: Pitchfork gave it 8.8 and ranked it No. 13 of 2023. Metacritic has it at 87 from nine reviews.
years.xp:
Album of the Year lists Pitchfork's score as 88, from Alphonse Pierre. PopMatters and The Line of Best Fit each gave it 90, Rolling Stone and The Guardian 80, AllMusic 70. The Needle Drop's Anthony Fantano scored it 50. The AOTY critic average was 81 from 11 reviews.

Pitchfork's 2023 year-end list put it at No. 13, between L'Rain's I Killed Your Dog and Olivia Rodrigo's GUTS, per BrooklynVegan. The Nation's Stephen Kearse wrote that it deals with celebrity, radical politics and her own contradictions 'with humility and openness'.

years.h: Sundial's cover is a hominin skull
years.p: The artwork is based on John Gurche's reconstruction of Homo floresiensis specimen LB1. [[Saba|057d211a-fba8-42d7-ad14-41f41d6f762f]] produced 'Balloons' and 'Toxic', and [[Common|c0a1179b-b14a-4d68-a3c1-1fdab16ed602]] guests on 'Oblivion'.
years.xp: The record has eleven tracks. Producers include Daoud, Gaetan Judd, Yussef Dayes with Wesley Singerman on 'Potentially the Interlude', Slimwav on 'Namesake', and Berg on 'Oblivion'. Guests: billy woods and $ilkMoney on 'Gospel?', Ayoni on 'Boomboom' and 'Oblivion', Jimetta Rose and Voices of Creation on 'Hold Me Down'.

years.cap: Noname at 43rd and Lake Park in Bronzeville, August 17, 2023
years.h: Common closes Noname's block party in Bronzeville
years.p: It is a parking lot at 43rd Street and Lake Park Avenue, with Navy Blue, Alex Vaughn and two DJs. Noname plays with a live band.
years.xp: CBS Chicago reports there was a supply giveaway. Noname told the station she wanted to celebrate with the community that raised her, and was planning her first Chicago bookstore within the year.

years.h: Tiny Desk again, with Saba and Smino back for one song
years.p: Six songs, mostly from Sundial. She closes with 'Balloons', which she jokingly calls her 'most controversial song'.
